newsitem.title: USA: Clinton acts to inform Medicaid patients fully.
newsitem.headline: Clinton acts to inform Medicaid patients fully.

text.p: President Clinton acted Thursday to ensure that poor people who receive government health benefits are fully informed about treatment options and urged Congress to give all Americans similar help.

Clinton, whose effort to overhaul the U.S. health care system collapsed in 1994, was responding to public concerns about rules of some managed care health insurance plans which prevent doctors and nurses from telling patients about alternate, sometimes more expensive treatment options.

He said he had directed the Health and Human Services Department to inform all state Medicaid directors that it is illegal to prohibit health care professionals from discussing any treatment option with their patients.

"Families facing illness simply should not have to worry that the doctor they trust does not have the freedom to tell them what they need to know. Patients have the fundamental right to know they are getting the best medical treatment, not simply the cheapest," he said.

Clinton said the same order had gone out to officials of the Medicare health programme for the elderly in December, and noted that he could act in these instances because Medicare and Medicaid "are federal programmes and the government is the largest purchaser of managed care" in the United States.
"To protect 130 million Americans enrolled in managed care throughout the private sector, Congress must act," he said.

A bipartisan bill to prohibit health plans from imposing so-called gag rules is currently pending. Clinton urged members of Congress to pass it without delay, saying "when they do so I will promptly sign it into law."

The American Association of Health Plans (AAHP), a trade organisation representing over 1,000 health maintenance organisations (HMOs) and similar plans, said it supported Clinton's position generally but had specific reservations.

"It is important to note that current legislative proposals go beyond the question of open discussions between patients and physicians about medical treatment options, and they would have unintended, adverse consequences if enacted as introduced," the association said.
Donald White, an AAHP spokesman, said the legislation as now drafted could keep HMOs from giving doctors "the latest research on better ways to practice medicine."
